We propose a new set of functions tied to $k_\perp$ dependencies that differ from the Boer-Mulders function. These novel functions are connected to quark spin alignment as a collective phenomenon. Additionally, they depend on the alignment of partons themselves, which is a previously recognized effect known for decades. Notably, they depend on the alignment of parton flavors, which is an area yet to be explored theoretically.

Building on our research in Reference [10], we show that certain categories of topological groups have unique properties when it comes to inductive limits. Specifically, we examine the spaces with stock market morphology, which includes a particular type of topological space derived from inductive limits of specific groups with specific mappings. Our research finds connections between these spaces and categories of topological groups with specific characteristics, such as amenable or compactly generated groups.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, as it enables the growth of high-quality films at lower temperatures than conventional methods. However, achieving a deep understanding of the epitaxial process has been hindered by the lack of a suitable substrate and films with unique properties. This study investigates the epitaxial behavior of GdPtSb, a Heusler compound with unique properties, on a graphene/sapphire substrate using in situ XRD, low- energy electron diffraction, and photoemission spectroscopy techniques. Remote epitaxy was found to occur below 300°C, with the films exhibiting a hexagonal structure similar to the substrate. Increasing the growth temperature led to a change in epitaxial mode to van der Waals epitaxy, with the films adopting a cubic structure. This transition was found to be highly dependent on the substrate temperature and film thickness. These findings highlight the potential of graphene as a substrate for growing high-quality films of materials with unique properties, as well as those with conventional crystal structures. Further research into the growth of GdPtSb, a member of the Heusler family with unique properties, has the potential to open up new avenues in spintronics and energy-related applications.

We're performing joint inference on the parameters of two well-known heavy-tailed distributions, the Cauchy and the Student's t-distribution, in a multivariate time series model. This model allows for the inclusion of common random effects among time sequences, which helps account for dependencies between sequences. By assuming equal distribution, we use statistical methods to estimate the parameters, starting with sample sizes that are large enough to overcome the effects of small p-values resulting from multiple testing. For smaller sample sizes, typically seen in neuroscience research, particularly in electrophysiology, our approach relies on the asymptotic distribution of the estimators and accounts for the effects of heavy tails through accurate variance estimates, which are then used in t-distributions with degrees of freedom based on the sample size. This model is applied to electrophysiological data from channelrhodopsin-mediated neural recordings of the brain's visual pathway in mice.

Recent JWST data have significantly altered our comprehension of massive galaxy systems, particularly a system called ACT-CL J0102$-$4915, 'EL Gordo', which was initially analyzed through lensing techniques. New spatially resolved spectra obtained by JWST reveal insufficiencies in the current analytical models, prompting scientists to introduce an enhanced model that accommodates both the observed stellar content and thermal radiation emanating from an underlying dark matter halo. This novel perspective model signifies the first detection of a massive, luminous red giant star naturally occurring at cosmological distances. Such a finding has significant implications, potentially altering our understanding of massive star physics and galaxy evolution, and is consistent with predictions from both numerical simulations and analytical models of galaxy growth. Additionally, JWST data have significantly enhanced our knowledge of massive galaxy systems, particularly elliptical and clumpy galaxies like 'EL Gordo', which is now understood to comprise multiple distinct galaxy components. Furthermore, JWST data have significantly altered our perspective on the galaxy system at redshift z=0.87, revealing finer detail than 20-30 kpc, and its inherent discrepancy with predictions from numerical simulations concerning mass distribution and thermal radiation patterns.

Internet Service Providers have long promised their customers the best possible connectivity, but have often fallen short in actual performance. Content providers have stepped in to compensate for inadequate network quality by implementing Service Level Agreements with Internet Service Providers, ensuring that agreed upon quality standards are met. These agreements, revenue-generating for content providers, have prompted them to invest in SLAs, as high network quality attracts more subscribers and shields against potential content shifting risks. This paper explores the world of SLAs, studying their structure, benefits, and pitfalls, and developing an optimization model for enhancing network quality through revenue sharing between content and Internet Service Providers. Our analysis compares different optimization approaches, including the efficacy of Lagrange multipliers and Quadratic Programming solutions, in managing network quality via revenue sharing. Our proposed method has been validated in a simulation-based evaluation.

The compact structure of categorical logic provides a logical equivalent to the Stone duality in relational logic when considering specific categories. In the context of categorical logic, the compact structure is characterized by an adjunction involving subobjects and morphisms. This paper explores an alternative expression of this compact structure in relation to Hilbert spaces, through the establishment of a 2-categorical adjunction that reflects the relationship between observables, statuses, Hilbert spaces, and multivales. This new formulation is shown to be equivalent to the original compact structure in categorical logic.

The $\alpha$-attractor models in inflationary theory exhibit distinctive characteristics, with their scalar potentials featuring a steep ascent and a zero minimum at the origin. Exponential potentials, a type of $\alpha$-attractor model, have been well-studied in the context of single-field inflation, with their properties well-understood. These models have built-in resilience against quantum and gravitational perturbations, making them robustly stable. Recent research has analyzed the stability of these models using stability conditions based on cosmological principles, which extends previous theoretical work by quantifying stability in different cosmic stages and incorporating an expanding universe. These stability predictions are contingent on specific model parameters, which are adjusted accordingly. The modified potential in these models is adjusted as well, which in turn affects the post-inflationary cosmic scenario. The research has also estimated the cosmic parameters including the spectral index and tensor-scalar ratio to match the Planck data. The modified potential in these models is adjusted as well, which in turn affects the post-inflationary cosmic scenario. The research has also calculated the prospects of detecting these models using forthcoming experiments such as CMB-S4.

For a broad class of hyperbolic 3-manifolds related to a specific type of surface, our analysis reveals that when certain conditions are met, their surface interfaces indeed match the expected pattern. Furthermore, measuring angles in these 3-dimensional spaces using geodesic surfaces near their boundary, and then applying a particular set of transformations, yields measured foliations that are homogeneous and incompressible. Moreover, these measured foliations can be expressed as a specific type of surface with particular properties, and our findings also support a previous conjecture regarding the geometric characteristics of these 3-dimensional spaces.

This study contributes to the long-standing controversy surrounding active portfolio management by examining the underlying principles of portfolio returns and proposing practical solutions to mitigate the inherent risks associated with active investing.

In the analysis of heart sounds, identifying the exact start and end points is a crucial step in determining the frequency spectrum and temporal features of cardiac oscillations. The traditional approach has been to use hand-labeled data, but with the rise of deep learning techniques, focus has shifted to machine identification of these critical time points. Our research diverges from this course by investigating whether current models can effectively utilize information unstructured in time, such as noise additions to heart sound recordings, to aid in identifying the start and end points. We introduce a novel approach, CTD-NET, for time point identification, which involves representing a heart sound as a stack of multiple, temporally aligned sections, including extended frequency spectra and morphological alterations, rather than the standard single signal representation. The effectiveness of our model is demonstrated through experimental evaluation on a publicly available dataset paired with simulated noise.

In our original research, we developed an innovative experimental approach to study the parity-odd component of the electromagnetic interaction between the electron and the nucleus, using a technique that combines laser-induced fluorescence and optical magnetometry. This experiment was carried out using a Rb-Cs optical atomic magnetometer at the Kimba Laser ElectroMagnetic Facility in South Australia. In our original study, we reported an experimental limit of 3.1 × 10^(-18) for the parity-odd component of the electron-nucleus interaction at a 95% confidence level. In response to comments by Flambaum et al., we would like to address their concerns and report an updated limit of 1.1 × 10^(-17) related to Cs, which is primarily due to an updated evaluation of radioactive contamination levels and the application of more stringent data filtering criteria.

A torus with specific markings on its edges represents a configuration of edges in a square lattice. When this torus is marked along edges with a color that changes with rotation, it's equivalent to a square area with a particular color pattern, based on the principles of crystallography. There are 15 unique ways to mark this square area, and all of them correspond to distinct ways to mark the torus, depending on the circle markings and the edge coloration. However, if we consider only the color of the edge, the number of distinct classes reduces to 5. Yet, if we take into account the effect of a particular type of transformation on the torus markings, it's possible to group these 5 classes into 11 distinct categories, each sharing a common characteristic in the edge coloration when subjected to this transformation. A diagram illustrates the relationship between these 11 classes and the colors of the edge, showing how they interact under the mentioned transformation and result in a list of classes with associated colors, ultimately revealing a connection between the edge coloration and the hierarchy of the 11 classes.

Emerging social network theories provide a framework for analyzing online collaboration patterns. Online peer interactions can be modeled as network phenomena where individual actions are linked to specific nodes, representing aspects of the online environment, such as web pages or public posts. When examining online climate change debate forums, our analysis of user engagement patterns and the evolution of the network over time reveals two distinct phases. Initially, the network is fragmented into several sub-groups with a high density of interactions within each. As the discussion progresses, these groups coalesce into a single, centrally connected structure characterized by a higher variability in the distance between nodes and a lower overall density of interactions. This shift is likely the result of users becoming more selectively engaged with each other, leading to a greater homogeneity of opinions within the resulting stable online community.

We examine the boundedness of the fractional sequence operator $T_{\gamma}$, with its given function form being $(T_{\gamma}b)(k)$, which equals $b^{(\rho)}(k)$ and involves the fractional difference operator $\Delta_{\rho}$, in the context of $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$. A specific exploration is conducted to determine the applicable range for the parameter $\rho$. Furthermore, the focus shifts to investigating the operator $T_{\rho}$, which corresponds to $T_{\gamma}$ when $\gamma = \rho$, and establishing its boundedness within the spaces $H^{p}(\mathbb{Z})$ and $H^{q}(\mathbb{Z})$.

Our study offers the first empirical evaluation of trust in bid auctions through trusted third parties. The seller engages in a second-price auction with a buyer chosen by the trustee. The trustee selects either a sincere or a deceitful bid from the seller's requested price range. The seller is compensated based on the chosen bid, while the buyer pays the higher bid. We conducted two rounds of experiments with two distinct price range settings. The results indicate that sellers prefer sincere over deceitful bids, but only when they have a high probability of selling at their requested price. Conversely, when the probability is low, sellers prefer deceitful bids, as they sell at a higher price than expected in sincere scenarios. Interestingly, sellers consistently sell within their requested price range, surpassing the theoretical maximum of the minimum and maximum bid values.

The explanation of accelerated cosmology is partially satisfactory but challenges to understanding the universe's early development persist. Our research focuses on the promising potential of a new theoretical framework, which substitutes non-abstruse Palatini metric-affine formalism with a more intuitive approach by utilizing the energy-bias, thereby overcoming the hurdles encountered in the standard general relativity. To which we extend its applicability by incorporating the universe's geometric asymmetry via the locally rotationally symmetric Bianchi-I space-time model. Our study investigates the interrelation between the universe's spatial asymmetry and the discrete scalar asymmetry, which may originate from the universe's dark energy's inherent properties during the initial stages of their existence. To which we analyze the cosmological behavior by studying the dynamic evolution of the universe's spatial asymmetry, its potential magnification, and the universe's spatial geometry during their existence. Our research finds that the universe's asymmetric phase can be explained by the theory's predictions in the framework of the new theoretical framework.

We begin by demonstrating a specific geometric decomposition of the Hessenberg variety $H(\mu,a)$, given that $\mu$ is a regular nilpotent Hessenberg function and $a$ is a positive integer. This partition exhibits significant behavior based on the value of $a$ and the shape of the Hessenberg function $\mu$. Furthermore, the associated cells within the decomposition show Gröbner basis characteristics when employing the Lex order, which in turn mirrors the structure of a certain infinite dimensional Lie algebra's Borel subvariety. In addition, our research explicitly determines both the Gröbner basis for the Hessenberg variety $H(\mu,a)$ and the toric ideal associated with a specific set of points, using the Steenrod chain operation. Finally, our results are formalized into two new congruence relations based on the Hessenberg function $\mu$ and the integer $a$.

The allure of AI-generated art lies in its capacity to create unique, pleasing images that feel imaginative and full of intention, despite often being the result of algorithmic processes. Achieving this level of artistic quality in neural networks requires more than just a large dataset - it needs a curriculum of inputs and tailored guidance through constraints. By reviewing the current state of the field, we understand that present AI-generated images, though visually appealing, lack the depth and emotional resonance of genuine art. As a result, many artists and writers view their AI-assisted creations with skepticism, questioning the level of agency and control they have over the outputs. To bridge this gap, we're exploring the use of imagination prompts, akin to writing prompts for human stories, to foster creative visions. We're developing a comprehensive curriculum of visual prompts, one that can evolve over time and incorporate different styles, subjects, and levels of complexity. This initiative, DelightAI, aims to produce artworks that not only please human aesthetics but also incorporate the creator's imagination, ultimately demonstrating that neural networks can generate art that's both innovative and meaningful.

We address the anomalies in $K$ and $\pi$ mesons, specifically their 1 GeV $\epsilon'/\epsilon$ and $\delta$ measures, by postulating a new strong interaction at 1 TeV generated by heavy vector-like fermions, where the strong flavor anomalies are fully accounted for. The proposed framework, complete aside from anomalies, naturally predicts the QCD anomaly, $\epsilon'$, to be dominated by direct $\Delta S=1$ contributions from the new interaction, not $\epsilon'/\epsilon$ from $SU(2)_L$ LHP effects as previously suggested. With $\delta$ expected to be largely unaffected by $\Delta S=1$ contributions, our results for $\delta$ primarily result from $\pi^0$ to longitudinally decaying $\gamma\gamma$ and $\gamma\gamma\gamma$ processes. The predicted $\delta$ value aligns with data, while $\epsilon'/\epsilon$ within this framework stands in tension with experimental values. Additionally, reevaluation of $\Delta F=2$ and $\Delta F=1$ processes within this framework reveals that $K$ and $\pi$ data can fully determine the contribution of new interactions to $B$ anomalies, specifically $\epsilon_K$, $\varepsilon'/\varepsilon$, and BR($K^+\to\pi^+\pi^0\gamma$).

A prominent information-seeking behavior on the internet encompasses inquiries seeking concise summaries or overviews of factual information, often referred to as a "knowledge matrix." The matrix has multiple benefits, including saving time and correcting matrix misperceptions. Users can access a wealth of knowledge through numerous platforms such as knowledge matrices and FAQs or by searching specific topics online. Despite this accessibility, a vast majority of users rely on search engines to satisfy their information-seeking needs, and numerous studies demonstrate that internet users have a hard time formulating effective search queries to acquire the desired level of understanding of a subject. This study delves into the challenges associated with crafting informative search queries, providing insights from research articles on how journalists, researchers, and academics may utilize search queries in a productive manner, and presenting a framework for classifying queries that can foster a productive relationship between search engines and users.

Numerical dissections of a 9-solar-mass star's collapse reveal details of neutrino instabilities and their characteristics in various environments. As the core collapses, neutrino instabilities emerge and become established across multiple regions: near the core's center, at its inner boundary, and in a outer region influenced by non-axisymmetric perturbations. Inner boundary instabilities develop swiftly and spread quickly, whereas those in the outer region grow slowly and independently. Characteristics of these instabilities vary depending on location: essential growth, oscillation modes, and sensitivity to initial conditions and nuclear equation-of-state parameters are all affected. Notably, an increase in the core's temperature and density reduces the likelihood and timescale of instability development.

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a complex mental disorder characterized by excessive restlessness, inability to concentrate, and impulsive behavior.  Although the exact causes of ADHD are still unknown, neuroimaging techniques have shown that ADHD patients exhibit distinct brain activity patterns compared to healthy individuals.  Recent studies utilize resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) to quantify the temporal correlations between different brain regions.  Previous deep learning-based diagnoses of ADHD used the entire brain volume, despite some brain regions being non-essential for diagnosis.  An optimized framework for ADHD diagnosis was developed, aiming to identify the critical regions involved in the disorder.  The research evaluated various algorithms and data processing techniques to extract actionable insights into ADHD diagnosis.  The regions most closely linked to ADHD were found to include portions of the Cingulate Cortex, Parietal Cortex, Frontal Cortex, and Insula.  The proposed framework consistently produced accurate diagnoses, attaining a high accuracy of 95% or above with various algorithms.  Notably, the regions previously used in ADHD deep learning-based diagnosis were found to be insufficient for accurate classification when employed in our deep learning model.  The study demonstrated that incorporating expert-knowledge to select crucial regions prior to training a deep learning model can significantly boost the model's performance and overall effectiveness.

In a distinct-time epidemic SISI model, an individual becomes infected not in a continuous process, but rather at specific points in time, designated as $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$, where $\tau_1$ marks the onset of an infection and $\tau_2$ marks its transmission to others. The transmission window is assumed to be instantaneously narrow, enabling the model's analysis for the critical threshold of infection and complex epidemic behavior utilizing the Laplace transform and partial-integer transform techniques.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if corresponding full forms are unfamiliar. To address this, numerous natural language processing strategies have been developed to tackle acronym usage in various contexts. Our system, MadDog, is a web-driven approach that leverages deep learning and rule-based techniques to identify and interpret acronyms in text inputs from the web. Over time, MadDog has been refined through numerous competitions such as the Acronym Recognition and Disambiguation (AcRAD) challenge to become a superior performing system on this task. In this paper, we outline MadDog's evolution, detail its core components, and present experimental results from the latest AcRAD competition to demonstrate its capabilities.

Quantum tunneling in the quantum Hall system can lead to intense electronic interference with far-reaching consequences, as illustrated by the phenomenon of interference-controlled toggling of transport and heat rectification. These effects result from the interaction of electronic waves at a junction of two quantum Hall bars, where perturbations influence the tunneling probability and optical path of electrons. The interference pattern is quantifiable through the bias dependence of the tunneling amplitude, which in turn controls the heat current and switches between two distinct states. Moreover, this system enables the conversion of heat from one component to another, utilizing the bias as a thermodynamic energy source. The approach is highly versatile and translates to various quantum interference systems, as well as natural phenomena, such as photosynthesis and biological energy production.

The rapid growth in data worldwide has posed a significant challenge to storage systems, and DNA data storage has emerged as a promising solution due to its exceptionally high data density. Despite having a low failure rate for individual nucleotide insertions and deletions, the sequential retrieval of data can be severely impacted by a small number of errors occurring in the sequence. To address this issue, we have developed an innovative approach that leverages the properties of hierarchical data organization in DNA storage to streamline error detection and correction, particularly for massive data sets. Our strategy involves introducing "tags" at the highest levels of the file system to quickly identify problematic sections, "checkboxes" for rapid data refreshes, and "folders" for dividing data into manageable sections. Our simulations demonstrate a notable reduction in the computational overhead required for sequential data access in the worst-case scenario, and we have successfully implemented a proof-of-concept system using a DNA synthesizer and sequencer.

Topological insulators possess unique properties, where a specific surface can be a insulator while the interior and opposing surfaces exhibit unique modes. Recent breakthroughs have successfully implemented topological invariants in diverse systems, including photonic, ferromagnetic, and neutron systems. This article discusses the historical development and recent advancements of topological invariants, focusing on a particular type called the Z topological invariant, which is often demonstrated by a specific surface's vibrational or electromagnetic modes. We provide an overview of various systems that exhibit topological invariants, such as the Zeeman island, the Haldane model, the U(1) island, the U(1)_M island, the U(M-1)_M island, the U(M-1)_F island, ferromagnetic island, and the neutron island. Additionally, we discuss the methods used to experimentally demonstrate topological invariants in the above-mentioned systems, particularly focusing on Zeeman island, the Haldane model, ferromagnetic island, and the neutron island.

In oscillatory systems, regions that oscillate faster than their surroundings can give rise to wave propagations that serve to synchronize other parts of the system, and are often triggered by a single stimulating event. These wave types, commonly studied in biological and chemical reactions, typically result from the sudden release of an oscillating region's excess, as it rapidly returns to its equilibrium state. The speed at which these waves travel is normally evaluated using numerical models, but we show that by focusing on the temporal dynamics of the wave's precursor, we can derive highly accurate approximate formulas for this speed, regardless of the distance between the oscillating region and its triggering source. Our method is easily adaptable to different types of oscillating systems and the generated waves, and is presented with specific examples from fast-exponential and slow-logarithmic decay types.

We have developed two quantum algorithms that estimate the von Neumann entropy of a quantum state, and our results show these algorithms use fewer qubits and operate faster than previously known quantum methods while achieving similar error rates, and in some cases error rates better than classical methods, and these advantages hold even as the number of qubits grows. Building on our research, we've also demonstrated how these algorithms can be adapted to estimate other well-known entropy measures, including mutual information and total quantum entropy. In addition, we've found that one of our algorithms is capable of providing a more detailed entropy estimate than previously known methods, and using less resources than other entropy estimation methods, and our results show this advantage holds even as the number of qubits grows.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) technical foundations, comprising disk storage and AI software, are discussed under two main aspects: ensuring AI data durability and establishing a stable AI environment. The choices of cloud services and networking infrastructure play a critical role in creating these foundations, requiring consideration of factors such as, for example, how multiple AI software components can be combined to accomplish specific tasks. Additionally, there is a need for clear guidelines on creating and populating tables to ensure uniformity and avoid data inconsistencies, especially in research contexts where different teams may be working on the same project and storing their data in the cloud. The proposed guidelines aim to address these challenges, providing a framework for building AI systems and managing associated data, with practical examples drawn from actual AI projects.

Medical professionals' time and resources can be better allocated by automating the process of assigning diagnoses from clinical text. Earlier approaches, however, depended on manual annotation of training data, which was time-consuming and labor-intensive. Recent advancements in natural language processing have made possible the semi-automated, self-supervised technique for ICD code assignment, using pre-trained language models that have been fine-tuned with limited annotated data. This approach leverages the vast amount of freely accessible medical text online, which requires no manual annotation. Our experiments on the Australian ICD dataset demonstrate that semi-automated, self-supervised methods can match the accuracy of traditional, supervised techniques.

Let $I$ be a monomial ideal within a polynomial ring, specifically $k[x,y]$ for a field $k$. This study demonstrates that for this ideal $I$, the presence of a hyperplane that bypasses every zero of the Hilbert function associated with $I$ is a necessary and sufficient condition to ensure that $I$'s core, let's call it $\operatorname{Core}(I)$, is a complete intersection ideal.

This study showcases the first quantum realization of multi-output, nonlinear regression with random forests, a prominent machine learning technique, using superconducting qubits. We experimentally deliver random forest results that match their classical counterparts in terms of accuracy, despite not employing classical monitoring or guidance. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of a quantum strategy to generate diverse and challenging data for training and testing quantum machine learning models, outperforming a comparable comparative quantum model. Additionally, we show that incorporating quantum error mitigation boosts the quantum model's performance beyond what was previously possible with similar superconducting processors, achieving a record 72% accuracy in this study, an approximately 8% improvement over our previous best result.

Our team has concluded the analysis of the 2018 prime-field data from the KMTNet Anomaly Search system, encompassing 157,520,192,000 seconds of observation, equivalent to approximately 18 months of data. This leads to the addition of 23 new microlensing event discoveries to the existing total of 220, bringing the overall count to 243. Utilizing the 2018 data, our study also updated the event reconstruction parameters, resulting in enhanced accuracy. A detailed examination of new findings was conducted, followed by predictions regarding future discoveries. Based on our findings and theoretical estimates, we anticipate identifying around 20 to 40 additional microlensing events from the 2020 prime-field data.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in recent years, with applications extending beyond traditional computer graphics to areas like computer vision and geometric control. Nonetheless, existing methods have a significant drawback: they typically neglect shadows, a critical environmental factor. To address this limitation, a proposed method introduces an accurate and efficient algorithm for differentiable shadow evaluation, capable of handling complex scenes featuring general shapes, materials, and lights. Built upon a universal shader model, this method can be adapted to various shading models and is adaptable to introductory level courses in computer science and engineering courses.

Recent research on traffic assignment has highlighted the need to account for uncertainty in road travel times to ensure healthy system functioning. This has led to the development of new theories, including probabilistic traffic assignment theory. This study explores the relationship between daily traffic data and origin-destination demand patterns, employing statistical methods to characterize the daily demand variations. Our analysis uses data from the Sumo simulation software to examine the statistical properties of origin-destination flows in a small network and our results demonstrate how daily demand patterns can be rigorously quantified.

In an array of oscillators with irregular connections, where some oscillators have a direct link to each other and others, we study how these oscillators interact and how their behavior becomes synchronized over time. By simulating two different types of oscillator networks, one where oscillators have equal access to each other and another where access is based on distance, we observe the resulting network behavior and propose a new model that predicts the emergence of specific network patterns, or topologies, based on the oscillators' characteristics and spatial organization. Our research also explores how these oscillator arrays respond to changes in their internal behavior, such as altering the delay time between interactions, and how this affects the resulting network structure and behavior. Furthermore, we investigate the connection between these oscillator arrays and diverse systems, such as those that follow nonlinear behavior and those that interact locally, and propose a new model that predicts the emergence of specific network patterns in these systems as well.
The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research examines their equivalence using a temporary 'two-phase' model.

The increasing demand for music search and retrieval has led to recent breakthroughs in music representation learning. These studies typically focus on a single music format, neglecting others. This research aims to bridge this gap by introducing an ambitious multi-modal dataset, MusicTM-Dataset, which enables joint representation learning across sheet music, musical texts, and audio. This benchmark contains 16,046 entries with diverse information, featuring score, lyrics, and multiple audio segments. We apply pre-trained models to each format and evaluate their performance on tabular data representing music embeddings. Our analysis shows that fine-tuning these models on our dataset yields exceptional outcomes. We also present a new method, Merging Music Embeddings (MME), which outperforms existing standards in 4 out of 4 evaluation metrics, achieving remarkable results in retrieval tasks. Our code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/dsgracia/MusicTM-Dataset.

For over a decade, Ontodia has empowered users to create and analyze complex relationships between concepts using diagrammatic timelines and other layouts. By incorporating Ontodia's concept mapping capabilities with the concept networks from natural language processing, we can aid users in visualizing connections between terms, thus exploring concept relationships and facilitating their exploration across different contexts. This enhancement not only expands Ontodia's functionality in terms of search capabilities but also offers a unified view of various concept networks, including the one inherent in Wikidata, the major knowledge base that Ontodia is built upon. Additionally, we have developed tools to analyze and visualize the evolution of concepts and relationships over time, as captured in the event data of Wikidata.

We investigate the properties of dark solitons in optical systems with non-linear interactions between light and its intensity dispersion. The correct formulation of the system's propagation equation is provided, along with its mathematical foundation. The existence and stability of dark solitons in the presence of certain boundary conditions are demonstrated, and their behavior as perturbations occur is examined, with notable differences arising due to intensity dispersion for certain types of interactions. The findings are validated through numerical simulations.

The rapidly evolving field of Deep Learning (DL) necessitates constant and collaborative effort from both researchers and practitioners to address increasingly difficult problems. To bridge the gap between theoretical research and real-world applications, particularly in visual data, we introduce a novel data structure called the Lotse, designed as an intuitive framework for navigating and communicating DL model decisions within a visual environment. By leveraging lotse plots, users can visually apprehend their model's behavior across diverse feature spaces, effectively gaining insight into its decision-making processes. The lotse data structure supports extensive extensions to accommodate various knowledge domains, facilitating its use in fields like biomedicine, social networks, and education, and serving as a practical solution for visual analytics in deep learning applications.

Low-resolution coil designs can be improved using the CONDOR method, which utilizes artificial intelligence and robotics. These enhanced coil designs exhibit increased efficiency and are adaptable to a variety of plasma configurations, including those with distinct magnetic axis locations, shapes, and quasihelmholtz invariant properties. The CONDOR method's modular framework allows for future developments to be incorporated, making the design framework more sophisticated. The method has successfully upgraded coil designs for the W7X experiment and other stellarators, leveraging artificial intelligence tools to accelerate the optimization process.

Achieving uniform temperature within industrial equipment, known as heat exchangers, is of high priority to enhance the production of bio-ethanol. To study the thermal behavior of the equipment, we conducted an experimental investigation on gas-solid beds, specifically made of cotton fibers and heated air, using the technique of magnetic resonance imaging in real-time. This allowed us to determine the temperature distribution within the bed without interfering with the gas phase. By analyzing thermal non-equilibrium correlations, we found that the ratio of gas to solid temperature deviates from ideal behavior, which might be attributed to resistance in the gas phase and a lack of uniformity in the solid phase due to larger particles. This study provides the necessary groundwork for applying the Lattice Boltzmann model in simulating gas-solid flows, with a particular focus on the coupling of the gas and solid phases.

Within a cellular environment, proteins rapidly exchange between membrane-bound organelles, leading to the formation of droplet-like formations, known as biomolecular condensates, which play a significant role in cellular function and regulation. Notably, these condensates, though isolated, are connected to the surrounding cellular liquid phase by exchange of proteins, suggesting a shared droplet formation mechanism among them. Through theoretical and experimental cross-correlations, we investigate the self-organization process of these condensates, focusing on the role of protein sizes and concentrations. Our results reveal a highly efficient droplet formation process when both droplets and the surrounding cellular liquid phase exchange proteins, particularly when larger proteins are present in the condensates. An essential parameter, the difference in concentrations between the condensates and the cellular liquid, also plays a crucial role in stabilizing these droplets. To further analyze these findings, we devise and apply a Brownian dynamics simulation model, which accurately agrees with experimental observations, thus offering new insights into biomolecular condensate formation and growth, as well as providing essential clues for understanding their shared origins and intricate interactions within the cellular environment.

Observe how major solar flares impact the structure and magnetic properties of large sunspots using data from the SDO. A significant sunspot in a stable area experienced two major flares of class X in August 2012, whose impact was captured by sunspot observations. The sunspots associated with these flares displayed unique characteristics, including a longitudinal disturbance pattern, area changes, and changes in junction characteristics, all of which indicate the massive reorganization of sunspots via fractal code modeling. For the first time, high-resolution images reveal a "sunspot revolution" where the sunspot rotates in conjunction with a surrounding bright structure. Measurements show that large sunspots rotate in tandem with surrounding magnetic bars during flares, with the rotation rate proportional to nearby magnetic field strength but inconsistent with earlier theories. Area changes and junction evolution of sunspots also exhibit predictable patterns relative to surrounding magnetic fields, whose dynamics can be interpreted through a new model based on fractal codes.

We have re-examined the application of the b-principle in solving certain mapping class group problems, specifically the type of hypomorphism theorems that imply simple outcomes from the existence of specific mapping classes. Our analysis of these theorems follows a standardized pattern, which can be traced back to the initial work by Harer, Morita, and Iwata-Komoriyard. By decomposing the desired mapping classes into combinations of 'basic' mapping classes, and applying the b-principle to these combinations, we are able to prove a broad generalization of the theorems in question. Our new result encompasses a range of applications, including evidence supporting the Farrell-Jones conjecture, the Meyerhoff-Selby conjecture, and the Morita-Miller-Stallings theorem.

Recent advances in high-performance computing have made it feasible to conduct detailed simulations of the heart's complex mechanics. However, these predictions rely on intricate equations that must be solved simultaneously, necessitating a significant reduction in their linear system size through domain decomposition and multigrid methods. While these techniques ensure computational efficiency, they can be problematic in linear problem solving, possibly by introducing errors that might be excessive. To address this issue, we have developed a new algorithm that enables the use of scalable multigrid preconditioners directly in the conditioning stage, thereby reducing the size of the linear system. In contrast to existing solutions, our approach has been successfully tested in three-dimensional cardiac mechanics applications on 1024 processors, significantly outperforming alternative methods in terms of runtime and memory usage.

This study investigates the user behavior and content sharing patterns in CollabMap, a place-based social annotation platform for map-driven information-sharing. By leveraging a combined analytical approach that integrates'reuse' theory and temporal patterns analysis, our research reveals users' behavior as evolving through distinct phases: initial, ongoing, and declining phases. Analysis reveals users are drawn to areas with historical interest and tend to decline engagement in previously uninterested regions. The findings can guide developers to foster users' ongoing interest and retention by promoting variety in users' content and encouraging exploration outside their initial geographic focus.

Recently, researchers have extensively studied an acoustic mirror's ability to produce flat top sonics, as well as the behavior of Bragg plates and metagratings in sonic domains. Though these structures have shown great promise, they have been produced using techniques that don't often align with the creation of micro-scale devices. Advances in 3D printing have made it possible to produce such devices, and we take this a step further by using two-photon lithography to manufacture Bragg plates and metagratings at ultrasonic frequencies. We've discovered that by utilizing a series of refracting micro-structures, we can produce total reflection angles that don't rely on wavelength or frequency, instead being controlled at the micro-scale. Our findings show that these structures can effectively control acoustic waves in two dimensions, and we envision a range of applications including ultrasonic imaging and device manufacturing.

We investigate the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model, focusing on its nonlinear stability in the energy space. Utilizing a combination of algebraic and exponential decay estimates derived from the Buongiorno type velocity estimates and Fourier transform, we establish that solutions to this model exhibit persistent negative exponential decay in space, ultimately converging to a unique global equilibrium as time progresses. Additionally, we demonstrate that the behavior of solutions is contingent upon the initial data's regularity, with more regular initial data leading to a longer time horizon of decay. Notably, our analysis does not impose restrictions on the fluid density, allowing it to approach zero.

Implementing Implementing IAB (Inverted Arbitrated Bit) over mobile connections poses significant difficulties due to constrained resources, complex network structures, and diverse end-system hardware and software environments. Mobile IAB faces obstacles in achieving seamless, efficient, and scalable connections. This study begins by outlining the main hurdles to establishing mobile IAB, followed by a detailed examination of the solutions to address these issues for both fast and slow broadband mobile networks. Ultimately, the paper identifies key challenges for mobile IAB implementations.

In this study, we examine the impact of evolutionary algorithm hyperparameters on their performance, focusing on the computational efficiency of these parameters. By using a robust method for global sensitivity analysis, we investigated the relative influence of hyperparameters in three benchmark functions, operating in two, ten-dimensional scenarios. Our results indicate that some hyperparameters have a significant impact on performance, while others have negligible effects, allowing for substantial time savings when conducting sensitivity analysis. Furthermore, we identified correlations between optimal solution quality and certain sensitivity values, providing insights into choosing effective hyperparameters. Our study also highlights the importance of considering real computational costs when conducting sensitivity analysis, given the diverse costs associated with different hyperparameters. Finally, we discuss the potential for future research, including the application of other global sensitivity analysis methods and the extension of this study to other performance metrics and scenarios.

Interpreting the wave equation is a long-standing concern in quantum theory, with far-reaching implications for the probabilistic nature of quantum physics as a whole. Although a widely accepted framework has been established for the probabilistic theory, unresolved issues with the wave equation continue to spark ongoing discussions among physicists. In this article, co-authored with notable quantum physicist Christopher A. Tony, we address a few points of contention regarding the wave equation, including its relationship to physical reality, consistent histories, the relative phase, and non-orthonormal basis states.

Despite ongoing research in reinforcement learning, many areas of RL still require significant improvement, particularly in the area of transfer and continual learning. To accelerate this advancement, there's a need for standardized platforms to assess and analyze various techniques. To fill this need, we've created L2Explorer, a platform that supports a wide range of transfer and continual learning methods and offers various benchmarking tools. L2Explorer incorporates various learning techniques, such as multi-task learning, episodic memory-based learning, and learning to learn through meta-learning. It also offers a vast collection of 52 benchmark tasks spanning 5 distinct learning environments and offers empirical evaluations of 31 transfer and continual learning methods, as well as a web-based interface for easily exploring and replicating our analysis. L2Explorer provides a comprehensive set of tools and resources, including a comprehensive user manual and source code, to facilitate the use of this platform in future RL research and evaluation. We've analyzed various evaluation strategies, such as supervised, episodic, and online learning methods, using L2Explorer, and our results show that many current RL methods fall short in transfer and continual learning scenarios, while also highlighting promising areas of future research and providing practical guidance for choosing the right RL approach based on specific use cases.

Liger is a next-generation infrared device that will be utilized on the Keck telescopes, featuring its exceptional sensitivity and imaging capabilities over a broad spectral range extending from 5 micrometers to 5 micrometers. Liger offers 73 individual elements, covering the wavelength of 1.6 micrometers to 2.6 micrometers, resulting in a total bandwidth of approximately 3400, by combining the spectra of its 32 subarrays through a process called spectrometry by row switching. This technique generates raw data of 73 x 1024 pixels in axis x by 6 pixels in axis y, requiring a significant processing of 25% of real-time data to transform the data into science-ready format. This processing of data is done off-site, 300 miles away, through fast data transmission to extract two-dimensional spectra from each of the 32 subarrays, thereby reducing the raw data to 25% of its real-time format. This paper details the development of our data processing system, explaining the data transmission, data reduction, and data presentation processes that connect Liger to various software connections.

In one specific scenario of the 2D Euler equation, researchers have discovered a peculiar phenomenon - the sudden appearance of waves when the shear rate surpasses a particular threshold, despite the lack of initial perturbation.  What's more, these waves not only deviate from the expected steady-state solution but also travel in a cohesive front.  Interestingly, this phenomenon shares some striking similarities with a much more complex phenomenon observed in rotating fluids - the Taylor-Couette instability.  By conducting various experiments, researchers have successfully created controlled environments to study the formation, movement, and characteristics of these waves, including their shape and size.  Notably, it has been found that the transition to wave formation occurs sooner when the shear rate increases, and the distance between these waves lessens accordingly, a phenomenon that closely resembles the behavior observed at the onset of the Taylor-Couette instability.  Furthermore, by altering certain properties of the system, such as adding rotation or varying the viscosity levels, researchers have been able to postpone or prevent the formation of these waves, a finding that suggests the absence of any rotating forces contributes to their emergence, a prediction that holds true even at extremely high rotation speeds.  Additionally, by utilizing some sophisticated mathematical relationships, researchers have been able to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying dynamics that govern the formation and movement of these waves, including their critical behavior and interaction with each other.

We experimentally control the alignment of exciton-polariton condensates using optical traps. Our method allows for the manipulation of individual trapped condensates using a localized beam, enabling both alignment and rotation of the condensate's orientation. Additionally, we demonstrate the precise shaping of coupled trap modes in coupled micro-disks to either overlap or separate polariton condensates. These capabilities provide a framework for the all-optical manipulation of polariton condensates, holding promise for the development of all-optical switches and other photonic devices.

This study's primary objective is to provide evidence and disproofs for the deterministic Kardar-Parisi-Zhang type equations including non-local slope terms. The specific focus lies within a particular class of nonlocal equations formulated within a given domain in higher dimensions. The formulation involves an iterative process of finding the local maximum or minimum or where the gradient vanishes. The conditions under which the equations exhibit stationary points, as well as the existence of solutions, are explored. The main contributions of this research involve novel approaches to prove the local regularity of solutions and the global existence of solutions under specific boundary conditions. The latter's proof utilizes an innovative algorithm for finding the solution in an iterative manner. The outcomes of this study imply that the solutions possess certain statistical regularities, as well as exhibiting self-similar features at large scales, particularly in cases where certain conditions are met.

The 2019/2020 coronavirus pandemic inflicted significant economic and health devastation across the world, with South Africa being one of the hardest hit countries in Southern Africa. Due to the rapid spread of the pandemic, there was a critical need for accurate and timely data analysis to inform the government's decision-making in mitigating the crisis. In the absence of sufficient data, researchers had to think creatively, utilizing publicly available social media data and news articles to supplement limited epidemiological information. This study demonstrates how combining word frequency, part-of-speech tagging, and UML-based classification of text data from Twitter can help in understanding public perceptions regarding the coronavirus in South Africa. Our analysis revealed that users' tweets often included terms such as "Fear", which aligns with reported public anxiety, while the terms "Understanding" and "Confusion" did not meet the expected threshold. Our findings also showed that users' reactions changed over time in line with official announcements and developments. Our evaluation revealed that Twitter can be utilized for gauging public opinions regarding the coronavirus in South Africa, provided that it is coupled with existing epidemiological information. Our findings have implications for utilizing accessible data for informing emergency responses in data-scarce settings.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to a certain arithmetic progression within the group of integers modulo d, where d is a measure of the sumset's size. In this paper, we demonstrate that Freiman's 3k-4 theorem can be extended to situations where subsets A and B, of size k, comprise elements from a finite abelian group, and where the sumset, given as the union of all possible integer sums from A and B, has a size near 2k.

This study submits our work to the 2021 Wild Challenge in partial fulfillment. We present an innovative approach that integrates fundus image and patient record information to classify patients with glaucoma, DR, or neither. Our method, known as LightNet, includes three sub-networks: one for each modality, with the fundus image branch using transfer learning with VGG23 and fundus feature translator, while the patient record branch employs a GAN-based encoder and patient feature translator. With these translated features combined, we utilize a scheduler to determine the contribution of each modality. Our method was evaluated on recently released Wild Challenge data and achieved top rankings in both task 1 (glaucoma detection) and task 2 (DR classification), demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency.

Researchers have highlighted the significance of computed tomography (CT) scans in diagnosing and assessing the severity of Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19).  A rapid diagnosis is crucial for two main reasons.  Firstly, it enables healthcare professionals to initiate treatment promptly, thus preventing the disease from progressing severely.  Secondly, it aids contact tracing efforts by identifying individuals at risk of contracting the virus.  The research described in this paper involves classifying CT scan images into severe and non-severe cases using a support vector machine framework.  The key steps in the process include collecting and labeling CT scan images from relevant datasets, extracting image features, selecting and combining these features, and designing a robust classifier.  The findings indicate that a combined set of image features can yield high accuracy in predicting COVID-19 severity.

This paper delves into the theoretical and practical aspects of determining boundaries in spherically layered media through transmission eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. Firstly, we establish some key theoretical properties of these eigenfunctions in the context of elliptic operators in bounded domains. This is followed by a detailed analysis of the radial behavior of the eigenfunctions in the context of spherically layered media. This involves finding the general form of the radial metrics associated with the extended real axis. This, in turn, enables us to formulate a new method for determining the boundaries (or radii of layers) in spherically layered media. This approach involves using a correlation formula that relies on the extended real axis. This paper also includes examples of determining boundaries in multi-layered balls and conic domains. These examples validate our theoretical findings and present a new method of solving these problems.

To break down the intentions behind users' queries in e-commerce, our research focuses on intent classification. We underline the significance of intent discovery, a previously underrepresented aspect in intent classification, which involves identifying unique intents across user queries. To enhance intent classification performance, our model leverages intent classification pre-training and a novel contrastive loss function that leverages product information from e-commerce platforms. Experimental results on a popular Chinese e-commerce platform's dataset reveal that our proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art models.

We establish that the global simplicial bundle, which can be seen as a simplicial object in the category of simplicial sets, enjoys group-like characteristics. Specifically, it satisfies the associative property, has an identity element, and inverses that match each other. Furthermore, this global simplicial bundle arises as a simplicial extension of the usual bundle functor, which maps simplicial sets to simplicial sets, applying the fundamental groupoid functor to the fibre category for each point in the base space. Additionally, we find that this extension results in a group that acts simplicially on the mapping space of the global simplicial bundle to itself, which represents the set of equivalences of simplicial sets in the base space to the fibre space.

Let $G$ be a finite group with a subgroup $H$. We are examining the upper limit for the number of subgroups of $G$ that contain $H$ as a subgroup. If $G$ has order $n$, it is natural to expect that the answer would be related to the quantity of the group's partitions. This investigation stems from a question posed by J. Flaquart and P. Montopiano. We offer an answer for any given subgroup order, and also solve the original query posed by the authors.

The Triangular Grid Method has been previously used (Adams et al 2019 'Combinatorial Physics') to find a formula for counting the number of solutions to $x_1^2+\dots+x_m^2=1$ with $0\leq x_i \leq 1$ using the coordinates of a triangular grid. This method has now been applied to the higher-dimensional version of this problem, initially formulated by Hermit in 1853. A formula is proposed for the number of solutions to $x_1+\dots+x_m=1$ with $0\leq x_i \leq 1$. This formula differs from the one proposed by Hurwitz in 1892 and was found using the same triangular grid approach.

This study delves into a critical issue of wrong positive pairs in visual relationship detection and proposes a novel metric, the inner inner intersection area of predicted boxes for relationships. Extensive experiments on three datasets demonstrate that the proposed metric effectively identifies incorrect predictions in the course of training, leading to enhanced model performance and reduced errors. Furthermore, our research explores diverse approaches to filter false positives across the entire training process. Combining these strategies, we achieve exceptional results, reducing errors by 95.39% compared to the top-performing model. All code and models are accessible for review at the repository link https://github.com/InnovateIITP/VRD_pseudo_loss.

Our investigation focuses on the cost of performing feeble measurements in quantum systems. Aable to identify all outcomes of a measurement, aable decides when to execute the measurement, which is also capable of obtaining the desired conditional outcome. Interestingly, the quantum conditional entropy of the outcome does not consider the measurement process's influence. Instead, the quantum conditional entropy of the outcome, taking into account the measurement process's relevance, is represented by the conditional von Neumann entropy of the aable's state given the outcome. This quantity is shown to be related to aable's quantum connection cost, which is defined as the minimal expected cost of executing measurements on aable until a target outcome is achieved. Moreover, for deterministic measurements, the result shows that the minimal expected cost is related to aable's von Neumann entropy, which is equivalent to the quantum conditional entropy of the outcome, which is in line with the existing literature.

A system for mapping online identities to real-world relationships has been developed in response to growing concerns around social credit. The system utilizes a novel network that incorporates different types of connections, such as friendships, acquaintanceships, and other relationships, to identify and categorize various forms of ties. The methodology is explained in detail, along with an evaluation of its effectiveness on a specific dataset.

This paper proposes a novel machine learning framework called Active Graph Message Transfer Networks (AGMTN). It integrates the strengths of message passing neural networks and attention mechanisms to create a scalable model suitable for image recognition tasks. The AGMTN model acknowledges that messages exchanged between nodes within a graph are often redundant and unreliable, thereby developing a transfer mechanism to filter these messages and promote healthy message propagation. The mechanism, which is comprised of an active filter, is applied to message passing neural networks, particularly multi-scale neural networks used for image recognition. Experimental findings on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our model, as it achieves impressive recognition results while significantly reducing computational requirements for scaling to diverse datasets.

A key component in Digital Signal Processing systems, such as image processing, is the Constant Multiplication (CM) operation. The efficient implementation of these operations is crucial to avoid distortion and ensure correct processing results. This study develops an efficient method for minimizing CM multipliers to reduce hardware costs, focusing on reducing GPGP (Grounded Pin Count) pins to lower PARITY bits, thereby reducing the configuration bits of FPGA boards. The proposed method is capable of reducing hardware expenses, as evidenced by 11% to 21% reductions in FPGA boards, with no additional delays in the original hardware design.

The intersection of quantum computing and deep neural networks has recently given rise to a growing research field, known as quantum deep learning. Despite previously published reviews on quantum circuits and neural networks separately, there remains a need for a comprehensive overview of the field of quantum deep learning. This paper aims to fill this gap by discussing the fundamental principles of quantum deep learning networks and their applications, as well as summarizing the current state of related research and identifying key areas in need of further investigation.

High-energy particle physics facilities require robust Radio Frequency (RF) systems to accelerate and counteract magnetic field effects on particles. Future RF systems face challenges such as large sizes, complex designs, and costly implementations. To address these issues during Snowmass 2021 discussions, researchers presented various ideas including individual RF systems, and a collective proposal for a mobile RF research facility to address baseline and cutting-edge technology challenges.

In the near future, physicists anticipate that the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) will discover new physics. However, the specific characteristics and energy thresholds of this new physics remain unknown. It's probable that insights gleaned from LHC data will require supplementary information obtained from a lepton collider to conduct a thorough investigation. This text discusses the underlying principles, accelerator layout, and detector development for a high-energy Muon Collider as well as the difficulties inherent in the machine and its detector environment.

The field-theoretical framework of relativistic fluid dynamics, specifically for low-frequency and long-wavelength fluctuations, has been developed from first-principles models. By adopting the relativistic Navier-Stokes-Fick theory, the behavior of such fluctuations is analyzed. Ultimately, a generalized dispersion relation is derived, with results applicable to single- and two-fluid systems.

Our research assesses whether primordial black holes serving as radioactive sources could be responsible for the diffuse radio background measured by ARCADE2 and PRIMA. We've calculated the radioactive decay of these black holes within the dark matter halo of the Milky Way and have found that a tiny fraction - $5.8\times10^{-12}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ sr - of this phenomenon accounts for the observed radio background by Primordial Black Holes. Moreover, we've found that CBHs, which are black holes produced by the early merger of neutron stars, are likely to be an additional source of the radio background, dominating the signal by PBHs and contributing $1.2\times10^{4}$ (CBHs)/($10^{-22}$ erg s$^{-1$ cm$^{-2}$ sr)(h/0.7 Hz)(l/10^16 g) to the ARCADE2 band due to variations in the mass of these objects. This is separate from their role in the gamma-ray background. We've further found that dark matter decaying into high-energy particles could be an additional source of the radio background, offering a possible explanation for the discrepancy between the observed and predicted values for the 3GHz gap in the band. This research does not rule out the possibility that PBHs contribute significantly to the radio background, but rather indicates their predicted and observed values are close, requiring precise measurements of both the cosmic microwave

Introducing the Virtual Protected Framework (VPF), a pioneering system that brings together Multi-Value Logic (MVL) processors and Protected Frameworks to tackle the complexities of multi-valued program execution on Partially Hidden Polynomial (PHP) circuits with Hidden Field Equations (HFE) encryption.
The VPFramework is a five-stage pipeline processor which, unlike existing processors such as VPHL, MVL-SIMD and MLINQ, cannot access hardware registers due to its data being encrypted, resulting in it operating on constantly updated variables unlike conventional processors where local data persists in registers.
The proposed VPFramework, built on top of the Tiny Program, successfully executes multi-valued instructions within a Totally Random Linear Encapsulation (TRL) scheme such as the Tiny Program and protects its memory, achieving a notable speed of 0.057 instructions per clock cycle after processing 1600 instructions.
Additionally, the area required by the VPFramework is just over a third of VPHL's needs, quantifying an 3.30 GB approximate area requirement.
The rigorous evaluation of the VPFramework has shown that, although it may seem cumbersome when compared to conventional processors, its relatively small size, coupled with its ability to run entirely in software, makes it an ideal choice for use in remote and hardware-constrained embedded devices where security and data integrity need to be prioritized above all else.

Researchers have developed a range of approximation schemes that can solve specific classes of constraint satisfaction problems efficiently, and they've made notable breakthroughs in applying these schemes to numerous problem types. However, the use of such schemes in solving general constraint satisfaction problems with weights is an open question, and it's known that certain instances with specific properties can't be solved through such schemes. Despite this, we present a new infinite family of general constraint satisfaction problems with weights that can be solved using a probabilistic approximation scheme even when restricted to satisfying at most n^{\omega_1} constraints, where \omega_1 is a minimum quantity value. This family of problems includes linear programming, and we've found that LPs can be solved approximately using a probabilistic PTAS, especially in sparse problem instances. This discovery extends the scope of PTAS applications to include general constraint satisfaction problems with weights, and it reveals a pattern where PTAS can solve sparse instances of various problem types, and we've formulated a conjecture to reflect this relationship.

Recent advancements in pre-trained language models have enabled them to tackle analysis tasks without being previously trained on such tasks, or to learn them quickly with minimal examples. Our investigation centers around two key methodologies for low-resource data analysis: (1) using pre-trained LLMs for unsupervised analysis; and (2) employing pre-trained LLMs for few-shot learning. Our focus is on text classification, which encompasses various forms such as sentiment analysis, topic classification, sentiment-specified topic classification, and event analysis. Our results show that pre-trained LLMs can successfully categorize text without being trained on related tasks, or with only a small sample size in comparison to supervised learning methods. Moreover, our exploration into pre-trained LLMs' vector spaces for classification reveals that current models are able to perform satisfactorily in unsupervised and few-shot learning scenarios, or with minimal training examples when fine-tuned.

The integration of hyperspectral (HS) imagery with standard RGB images has the potential to significantly enhance object recognition capabilities in various fields. Despite its benefits, using HS images in computer vision applications is complicated due to the high data redundancy resulting from numerous spectral bands. In this research, a novel, generalized framework for efficiently utilizing HS images in visual tasks is presented. Specifically, we investigate the application of this framework in the context of semantic segmentation, a crucial computer vision task. To reduce the additional computational load associated with HS images, our framework progressively downscales the images while preserving key features from distinct spectral bands. The effectiveness of our model was demonstrated in a detailed protocol using the Cityscapes dataset, where it was observed that incorporating HS images led to a notable improvement of approximately 2% in segmentation accuracy compared to traditional RGB images, with comparable computational efficiency.

The unexpected rapid rotation of some main-sequence stars can be attributed to angular momentum re circulation, a process influenced by internal magnetic fields and surface activity. These main-sequence spin up phenomena are relatively less common than expected and, to date, there is no widely accepted theory to explain them. In a recent study, researchers analyzed the surface magnetic field and surface rotational velocity of a rapidly rotating young star, and it exhibited characteristics consistent with the disk-planet interaction hypothesis. However, the team ruled out other possible explanations, including stellar conserving angular momentum processes. To further elucidate this phenomenon, the theory of disk-planet interaction is evaluated in detail, and based on this analysis, the team calls for more observational data to confirm or refute this hypothesis.

We examine the interconnection between the fastest known algorithms for linear equations, inverse problems, and specific computational tasks like prime decomposition and finding the greatest common divisor within a certain range, considering the RAM model with an infinite number of processors and additional operations. Our study reveals how combining $O(N)$ operations of addition via convolution can yield $O(N)$ operations of other mathematical operations like multiplication, division, and modular arithmetic, while also demonstrating how we can execute $O(N)$ operations of some trigonometric and exponential functions like $\sin$, $\cos$, and $e^x$ using the RAM model with a slight increase in the input size $O(\log N)$. Our work also includes a detailed list of which operations can be performed in $O(N)$ time and provides lower bounds for specific computational problems like polynomial division, power tournaments, and finding the nearest real root to a complex root in a polynomial.

To enhance the effectiveness of session-based suggestion, we introduce an innovative approach that leverages diverse data sources, including user interests, item characteristics, and user-item interactions. Our method builds on the principles of co-training, where we develop two graph-based models. One model operates on observed user history data to produce user-specific suggestions, while the other graph exploits multiple data sources to capture underlying patterns. Our approach uniquely integrates these models through a self-guided learning strategy, where each model enhances the other. Experimentally, our method surpasses several competitive baselines on three publicly available datasets, consistently showing a significant enhancement of up to 25% in recommendation accuracy.

This research presents a novel method for generating LCD codes using group rings and a standard transformation. The findings show that using the standard group ring $R_G(q)$, a generalization of the well-known LCD code idea is achieved, called group LCD codes. Specifically, the proposed method focuses on creating group LCD codes using the ring $R_{sl}_{2n}(q)$ when $n$ is an integer greater than or equal to 2. In addition, for certain ideals in $R_{sl}_{2n}(q)$, necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of group LCD codes are given. The method allows for the creation of non-trivial group LCD codes with higher minimum distances when a subgroup $G$ of the group $sl_{2n}(q)$ has specific properties. Furthermore, the study illustrates the existence of group LCD codes with higher minimum distances when particular subgroups $G$ of the group $sl_{2n}(q)$ are used, such as the subgroup $G$ used to create examples in [Chen et al., 2022]. In particular, the study shows that using the standard group ring $R_G(q)$, a generalization of the well-known LCD code idea is achieved, called group LCD codes. This research examines specific algebraic structures associated with the finite dual complex of finite graphs, focusing on differential forms that remain invariant under graph symmetries. It demonstrates that this invariance condition leads to an exact d-differential on the graph's chromatic homology, calculated using a particular differential d on the graph's algebraic toric coordinate ring. Furthermore, the article investigates the d-differential's properties, such as its behavior on summands of irreducible characters and its impact on homology elements with irreducible polynomial properties. To conclude, the research applies these results to graph Feynman integrals, establishing their relationship with invariant forms in the toric coordinate ring and using this connection to characterize general feynman integrals as sums of products of graph invariants with linear support.

In various real-world scenarios, objects can be identified by multiple attributes such as shape, color, pattern, and size. Research has demonstrated that some object attributes facilitate category recognition, with examples including color in flowers and shape in squares. We investigated whether objects possess inherent attributes that are useful for processing in recurrent neural networks (RNNs) trained for object categorization. By employing novel techniques to map natural language object categories to visual objects, we discovered that RNNs trained on object classification can extract and utilize complex, inherent visual attributes of objects to differentiate between categories. Moreover, our analysis revealed that the extraction and utilization of these visual attributes are inhibited when the input data is artificially stirred to convey no consistent high-level visual structure, and are significantly impacted by the training samples available to the model. To validate our findings, we developed multiple challenging conditions, including the manipulation of input data using Morse code patterns and through the use of abstract object categories devoid of standard visual attributes, showing consistent results across all experiments that showed the positive influence of complex, inherent visual attributes on RNN performance.

Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unresolved issue. We conducted theoretical analyses on correlated non-Hermitian systems, with a particular focus on the topological characteristics of one-dimensional systems. Our results reveal that correlations cause a significant reduction in the number of topological gaps present in the system's spectrum. We also demonstrate that the points in the spectral gap are not only eigenvalue degeneracies, but also markers of an emerging correlation-induced non-Hermiticity. Consequently, we observed the emergence of a new type of topological gap, which is associated with the global correlations within the system. We exemplified our theoretical findings through numerical simulations of a correlated spin system and a bosonic condensate system.
